note: Interview-style scenario walkthroughs. Each gives a problem, an expected approach, and a grading rubric. There is no single correct answer: the rubric grades the reasoning, the tradeoffs named, and the verification step — not a memorised phrase.

expected_approach: Start from requirements: traffic shape, data durability, recovery objectives — ask clarifying questions before drawing boxes.
Place a load balancer in front of stateless web instances across at least two Availability Zones.
Put the application tier in private subnets and the database in isolated subnets, reachable only from the application tier.
Store uploads in object storage and sessions in a shared store so instances stay stateless.
Name the failure modes: zone loss, database primary loss, load balancer target failure — and the mitigation for each.
Describe how you would prove it: health checks, a zone-failure game day, and validation against real state.
pitfalls: Drawing boxes before asking a single clarifying question.
One Availability Zone with a promise to add a second later.
State on the instance disk, which makes scaling and replacement impossible.
walkthroughs.problem: Design a web application that serves 10,000 concurrent users, must stay up if an Availability Zone fails, and stores user uploads and a relational dataset. Walk through the architecture, the failure modes, and how you would prove it works.

rubric.good_looks_like: Asks about traffic, data, RTO/RPO and budget instead of drawing immediately.

rubric.criterion: Uses zones, tiers and trust boundaries correctly
rubric.good_looks_like: Public web tier, private app tier, isolated data tier; at least two zones.
Sessions and uploads live in shared stores, not on instance disks.
Zone loss, primary loss and target failure each have a concrete answer.

rubric.criterion: Describes verification, not just the design
rubric.good_looks_like: Health checks, game days and validation against real state.

walkthroughs.title: Design a highly available web application

expected_approach: Stabilise first: stop the retry storm from making it worse, and communicate status.
Separate client latency from server latency: compare load-balancer latency with application request duration.
Check one layer at a time — load balancer targets, application, database — with that layer's own metrics, not another layer's logs.
Look for the single slow component: one target group, one zone, one replica.
Form a hypothesis, test it with a targeted check, and only then act.
After the fix, verify with the same metrics and record the timeline.
pitfalls: Believing the first log that names a culprit.
Restarting everything and calling it fixed without knowing the cause.
Debugging for an hour without telling anyone the service is down.
walkthroughs.problem: Checkout latency jumps from 300 ms to 5 seconds. The application logs blame the database, the database logs blame the network, and the load balancer reports timeouts. Users are retrying, which doubles the traffic. Walk through how you find the cause.

rubric.criterion: Stabilises and communicates before deep debugging
rubric.good_looks_like: Mentions mitigating the retry storm and telling users what is happening.
Does not take one layer's logs as proof about another layer.
Per-zone, per-target-group, per-tier comparisons.
States what would confirm or refute each hypothesis.

rubric.criterion: Verifies the fix and records the timeline
rubric.good_looks_like: Same metrics after the fix, plus a timeline for the review.

walkthroughs.title: Debug a production outage with conflicting logs

expected_approach: Start with discovery: inventory every server, application, dependency and data flow before choosing anything.
Score workloads on cost, criticality and coupling, and find the ones to retire.
Choose a strategy per workload — rehost, replatform, repurchase, refactor, retire, retain — and say why for each.
Plan in waves ordered by dependency, easiest first, so the team learns the process on low-risk moves.
Design the cutover: parallel running, continuous replication, gradual traffic shift, tested rollback.
Cover data verification, decommissioning, and the landing zone the workloads move into.
pitfalls: Choosing one strategy for all 40 servers.
A big-bang cutover weekend with no rollback.
Forgetting the reporting job that reads the production database directly.
walkthroughs.problem: A company has 40 on-prem servers running a mix of web applications, a reporting database and file shares. They want to move to the cloud in six months. Walk through how you plan the migration.

rubric.good_looks_like: Inventory and dependency mapping come before any strategy choice.
Different strategies for different workloads, each justified.
Easiest, lowest-risk waves first; dependent workloads move together.
Parallel running, replication, gradual shift, tested rollback.
Verification of data, old-estate retention and decommissioning plan.

walkthroughs.title: Plan an on-prem to cloud migration

expected_approach: Attribute first: split the bill by tag, service and team to find which line actually grew.
Check the trend, not just the month: when did the growth start, and what changed then?
Look for the usual causes: an oversized instance, a forgotten test environment, a runaway job, data transfer, orphaned storage.
Verify with utilisation evidence before changing anything — do not delete on suspicion.
Fix the cause, then add the guardrail: budget alerts, tagging policy, scheduled shutdowns, a monthly review.
Communicate what happened, what it cost, and what changed, in plain language.
pitfalls: Deleting resources on suspicion without evidence.
Optimising the most visible line instead of the biggest one.
Fixing the bill and adding no guardrail, so it happens again.
walkthroughs.problem: The monthly cloud bill doubled. The finance team wants answers and the engineering team says nothing changed. Walk through how you find the cause and stop it happening again.

rubric.good_looks_like: Tags and per-service split locate the growing line first.
Finds when growth started and what changed at that time.
Utilisation data before any deletion or resizing.

rubric.criterion: Adds a guardrail, not just a fix
rubric.good_looks_like: Budget alerts, policies or shutdowns that stop recurrence.
Plain-language summary of cause, cost and prevention.

walkthroughs.title: The cloud bill doubled overnight

expected_approach: Define the stages: checkout, build, lint, unit tests, integration tests against real services, packaging into one immutable artifact.
Promote the same artifact through staging to production; never rebuild per environment.
Put an approval gate between staging and production with the staging evidence attached.
Design rollback before the first deploy: keep the previous artifact, make the traffic shift reversible, keep database changes expand-then-contract.
Record the audit trail: who approved, what version, when, and the test evidence for that version.
Add deployment monitoring: error rate and latency gates, alerts linked to the rollback runbook.
pitfalls: Rebuilding the artifact for production.
An approval gate with no evidence attached to approve against.
A rollback plan invented during the first bad deploy.
walkthroughs.problem: A team ships a customer-facing application and must prove every production change was tested and approved. Design their CI/CD pipeline: stages, environments, approvals, rollback and audit trail.

rubric.criterion: Covers the full pipeline with evidence at each stage
rubric.good_looks_like: Build, test, package stages each record what ran and what came out.
Same artifact in staging and production; config injected per environment.
A recorded human decision with test results and plan attached.
Previous artifact kept, reversible traffic shift, compatible database changes.
Who approved what and when; error-rate gates and alerting.

walkthroughs.title: Design a CI/CD pipeline for a regulated team

expected_approach: Treat it as an incident: correlate the signals, confirm with the instance's own logs and metrics.
Contain first: isolate the instance by cutting its network path, revoke the exposed key, snapshot the disk before touching anything.
Investigate from the preserved evidence: timeline, entry point, what was accessed.
Eradicate the cause: rotate credentials, close the hole, rebuild from known-good images — do not clean in place.
Recover in stages and verify with the same signals that detected the incident.
Write a blameless review with actions, owners and dates.
pitfalls: Deleting the instance immediately and destroying the evidence.
Deleting the suspicious process while the stolen key still works.
Cleaning a compromised system in place instead of rebuilding it.
walkthroughs.problem: An instance is making outbound connections at 3 a.m. to an unknown address, and an access key has been used from two countries at once. Walk through the incident response.

rubric.good_looks_like: Odd egress plus key reuse plus timing form the picture.
Isolate, revoke, snapshot — in that order.

rubric.criterion: Eradicates the cause, not the symptom
rubric.good_looks_like: Credential rotation, hole closed, rebuild from image.
Restricted network first; same detection signals checked quiet.
Timeline, root cause, actions with owners and dates.

walkthroughs.title: Respond to a compromised cloud instance

expected_approach: Check the current headroom and the scaling limits: instance caps, database connections, load balancer targets.
Scale the stateless tiers first — they scale horizontally — and pre-warm what cannot scale fast.
Protect the database: connection limits, read replicas for reads, caching in front of hot queries.
Shed load gracefully if needed: degrade non-critical features rather than failing all requests.
Watch the right metrics during the spike and keep a rollback for any change made in a hurry.
Afterwards: make scaling automatic, load-test to the new peak, and record the runbook.
pitfalls: Scaling the database the way you scale the web tier.
Raising limits without checking what breaks first.
Making hurried changes with no way back.
walkthroughs.problem: A marketing campaign sends ten times the normal traffic to the application with two hours' notice. Walk through how you keep the service up, and what you change afterwards so the next spike is boring.

rubric.good_looks_like: Instance caps, connection limits and target health before scaling.

rubric.criterion: Scales stateless tiers, protects the database
rubric.good_looks_like: Horizontal scaling for web/app; connection limits and caching for the database.
Non-critical features degrade instead of all requests failing.

rubric.criterion: Watches metrics and keeps changes reversible
rubric.good_looks_like: Monitors during the spike; hurried changes can be rolled back.
Autoscaling, load tests, runbook updates.

walkthroughs.title: Handle a 10x traffic spike

expected_approach: State RTO and RPO as numbers, and tie them to the cost of downtime the business already accepts.
Present the strategy that fits those numbers — backup/restore, pilot light, warm standby or multi-site — with its cost.
Show the tradeoff explicitly: what a faster recovery costs, and what a slower one risks.
Explain how failover is triggered and who can declare a disaster, with named people and thresholds.
Prove it works: game days, rehearsal results, measured recovery times — not a document that was never run.
Cover the return to normal: failback, verification, and the post-incident review.
pitfalls: Quoting RTO/RPO as adjectives like fast or minimal.
A DR plan that has never been rehearsed.
Hiding the cost of the standby from the business.
walkthroughs.problem: You propose a disaster recovery plan to the business. They ask: how long will we be down, how much data will we lose, what does it cost, and how do you know it works? Walk through your answer.

rubric.criterion: States RTO and RPO as numbers tied to business cost
rubric.good_looks_like: Numbers, not adjectives, linked to what downtime costs.
The chosen strategy is justified by the RTO/RPO, not by preference.
Faster recovery costs more; the tradeoff is explicit.

rubric.criterion: Names who declares and how failover triggers
rubric.good_looks_like: Named people, thresholds, automatic where possible.
Game days and measured recovery times, not an untested document.

walkthroughs.title: Defend a disaster recovery plan
